subsection: 6. Fats and oils as a food commodity

notes.h: Nutritional significance of fats and oils
notes.b: Fats and oils are the most concentrated fat foods in the diet. Knowing what they supply, and what they leave out, explains how they should be used and chosen.
points: Fats and oils are almost pure fat, supplying 82–99.9% fat. Butter and margarine are about four-fifths fat or more and oils are almost pure fat, so the balance is mostly water in butter, margarine and spreads, and water varies inversely with fat.
They supply energy at 37 kJ or 9 kcal per gram, which is more than twice the energy in a gram of protein or carbohydrate, so a small amount of fat adds a lot of energy.

They supply fat-soluble vitamins (those that dissolve in fat, not water) and fatty acids. Butter has vitamins A and D naturally, vegetable oils supply vitamin E, and essential fatty acids (ones the body cannot make) come from plant oils.
Margarine and spreads are usually fortified with vitamins A and D, which are not naturally present in plant oils, so they match the vitamins that butter provides.
They supply little or no protein, carbohydrate, fibre or minerals. Butter and margarine contain traces of minerals such as calcium and sodium (from added salt).
Spreads contain water as well as fat, so a lower-fat spread contains more water than a butter or margarine of the same type.

The type of fat depends on its source. Animal fats (butter, lard, dripping) are saturated and raise LDL (the 'bad' cholesterol), olive oil is monounsaturated, and plant and nut oils are polyunsaturated.

Spreads and oils are eaten daily but in small amounts, yet much of the fat in the diet is hidden in processed, convenience and takeaway foods, meat products and dairy, so total fat intake is greater than the visible fats suggest.
In the Food Pyramid, fats, spreads and oils are used sparingly, choosing mono- or polyunsaturated types.
notes.tip: For a question on nutritional significance, give the fat content (82–99.9%), the types of fat by source and their effect on LDL and HDL, energy, insulation, organ protection, fat-soluble vitamins, and the small amounts of protein, carbohydrate and minerals.

notes.h: How butter, oils and margarine are made
notes.b: The three main commodities start from different raw materials. Butter comes from milk, oils from plants, and margarine from plant oils that are then hardened.
points: Butter is made by churning cream. The fat droplets clump together, the buttermilk is drained off, and the butter is worked and salted or left unsalted.
In the EU, butter is at least 80% and under 90% milk fat, with at most 16% water. It is an animal, saturated fat and a water-in-oil emulsion (tiny water droplets spread through the fat).

Oils are pressed or extracted from seeds, nuts and fruits such as olives, rapeseed and sunflower. They are then refined (cleaned, bleached and deodorised) to remove impurities, giving a bland oil with a higher smoke point (the temperature at which it starts to give off smoke).
Extra virgin olive oil is made from olives by mechanical pressing without chemical refining, so it keeps its flavour. It is used for dressing and gentle cooking.
Margarine and spreads are made from vegetable oils, and sometimes fish oils. Spreads are lower in fat than margarine and butter and contain more water.

The types on sale are butter, margarine, low-fat spreads, functional dairy spreads (cholesterol-lowering), blended spreads (butter with vegetable oil), oils (olive, rapeseed, sunflower, vegetable), lard, suet, dripping and cooking fat.
notes.tip: Do not say margarine is made from butter. Butter is an animal fat made by churning cream, margarine is made from vegetable oils, and spreads are not all margarine.

notes.b: The right fat depends on what it is for, what the label says and your health needs. Reading the label first makes each choice easier.
points: Read the label for the type of fat, ingredients, energy per 100 g, total fat, saturates, salt, additives and allergens (milk, soya).
The ingredients list shows the largest ingredient first, so a spread listing water or vegetable oil first contains mainly those.
Choose by health: more mono- and polyunsaturated fat and less saturated fat. Olive or rapeseed oil are healthier choices, and low-fat or functional spreads suit people watching weight or cholesterol.

Choose spreads with few hydrogenated fats in the ingredients list when reducing trans fat (a fat formed during hydrogenation that is harmful to the heart) in the diet, and avoid partially hydrogenated fats.
Choose by use. Oils have higher smoke points than butter, so oils suit frying and butter suits spreading and baking.

Hard margarine or block fat suits pastry and creaming because it is plastic (firm yet workable) at room temperature. Low-fat spreads are unsuitable for cooking and baking because of their high water content.
Other factors are cost, taste, dietary needs (dairy-free, vegan, allergy), brand, packaging, shelf life, organic, and whether it is Irish (the Bord Bia quality mark).
notes.tip: Questions on choosing fats ask for factors such as choosing low-fat foods, avoiding hydrogenated fats, comparing labels and traffic lights for saturates, and choosing fat-free or low-fat dairy.

notes.b: Fats spoil in two ways, which is why storage advice differs. Air, light and heat make fats go rancid, while fat also soaks up smells from other foods.
points: Rancidity (the off smell and taste of spoiled fat) is the main storage problem. Oxidative rancidity is caused by air, light and heat, and hydrolytic rancidity by water breaking down the fat.
Store fats and oils in dark or opaque, airtight containers in a cool place, away from light and heat, to limit oxidative rancidity. Buy sensible quantities and use them before the date.
Store butter and spreads in the refrigerator, with a cover or in the original wrapper or tub, because fats absorb strong odours such as onion and fish. Freeze butter for longer storage.
Store nuts and seeds in airtight containers in a cool place, because their oils go rancid quickly.
Oily fish and fatty meat are stored in the fridge and used promptly, or frozen.
Keep used frying oil covered and strain it, so food particles do not speed up its breakdown. Do not top up old oil, and discard it when it is dark, smokes at a low temperature or foams.
Foods that contain fat, such as pastries, cakes, biscuits, crisps, nuts and whole-grain flours, are kept in airtight tins or packs.
notes.tip: Keep the two causes apart. Oxidative rancidity (air, light, heat) is why oils are stored in the dark, and odour absorption is why butter is kept with a cover on in the fridge. Exams also ask why frying oil is strained.

notes.b: How fat is handled in the kitchen changes both the energy in a dish and how it turns out. Some methods add almost no fat, while others depend on it for texture.
points: Methods that add little or no fat are grilling, steaming, poaching, microwaving and baking on a rack. Trimming visible fat from meat before cooking reduces the fat in the finished dish, as does removing skin, using a non-stick pan and cutting the fat in recipes.
Frying adds fat and therefore energy, because the food absorbs fat. Shallow frying uses a little fat and transfers heat evenly to food, giving it a golden colour.
Deep-fat frying in a deep pan at the correct, controlled temperature limits the amount of oil that food absorbs. Do not overheat the oil, and drain the food on absorbent paper.
Creaming butter or margarine with sugar traps air in the mixture, giving cakes a light texture.
Rubbing fat into flour makes shortcrust pastry. The fat coats the flour proteins and limits gluten, which shortens the pastry. Fat is layered in flaky and puff pastry.

Fat is also used for frying and roasting (heat transfer and browning), greasing tins, emulsions such as mayonnaise, hollandaise and dressings, roux and sauces, and for flavour, richness and moistness.
Fat from roasted meat collects in the tin and can be strained and used as dripping for frying.
notes.tip: Questions ask how fat is used in pastry (shortening) and in cakes (creaming), and for three ways to cut fat: lean meat, trimming fat, low-fat products, grilling or steaming instead of frying, and avoiding takeaways.

notes.h: Effects of heat on fats, and processing
notes.b: Heat changes fat, and not always for the better. Knowing what happens when fat is overheated, and how manufacturers process fats, explains the safety rules and the labels.
points: Fat melts when heated, but overheating breaks it down (its smoke point is reached and acrolein, an irritant, forms). Repeated heating lowers the smoke point and produces off flavours.
Fat that reaches flash point (the temperature at which it ignites) can catch fire, so never leave a deep-fat fryer unattended.

Processing includes refining, hydrogenation (turning oil into fat), blending, emulsifying, and adding vitamins and colour. Hydrogenation can form trans fatty acids, and the EU limit is 2 g per 100 g of fat.

notes.h: Production of margarine, with packaging and labelling
notes.b: Margarine is made by turning liquid vegetable oil into a spreadable solid fat and mixing it with a water phase. The stages must be written in order.
points: 1. Extract the oil from seeds such as sunflower, rapeseed, soya or palm, then refine it to remove impurities.

2. Hydrogenate it. Hydrogen gas is passed through the heated oil in the presence of a nickel catalyst (a substance that speeds up the reaction), which adds hydrogen at the double bonds and makes the liquid oil a semi-solid fat. The catalyst is then removed.
3. Blend the hydrogenated fat with other oils to give the texture (plasticity) and spreadability needed.
4. Prepare the water phase from water or skimmed milk, salt, colour (carotene), flavour and vitamins A and D. Lecithin is added as an emulsifier, which keeps the fat and water from separating.
5. Emulsify by mixing the fat and water phases, with churning, to form a stable water-in-oil emulsion.
6. Chill rapidly in a votator, a scraped-surface heat exchanger, while working the mixture so that a plastic, spreadable fat forms.
7. Weigh the margarine and pack it in foil-wrapped blocks or plastic tubs. An airtight, light-proof pack protects the fat from oxidation and absorbed smells.
notes.tip: Hydrogenation hardens oil by adding hydrogen to double bonds, to make the fat plastic and spreadable and to improve shelf life. Write the stages in order.

notes.b: The label tells shoppers what is in the pack and how to store it, and the law sets out what it must show.
points: The label gives the name and type (margarine or spread), and lists the ingredients in descending order by weight with allergens such as milk and soya highlighted.

It also gives a nutrition declaration per 100 g (energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, salt), the net quantity, a date mark (best before) and storage instructions, the manufacturer's name and address, and the country of origin and batch (lot) code.

In Ireland, food labelling follows Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 as given effect by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014, with the FSAI giving guidance on food safety and labelling.
notes.tip: Margarine and butter normally carry a best-before date, not a use-by. Ingredients are listed in descending order of weight, and allergens are highlighted in the list.

notes.b: Low-fat spreads and functional spreads are different products for different needs. One lowers the fat in the diet, and the other lowers blood cholesterol.
points: Low-fat spreads have about half the fat of butter and more water, so they are lower in energy and suit a calorie-controlled diet.
Low-fat spreads are made from vegetable oils, water and milk proteins, and are low in saturated fat and high in unsaturated fat.
Low-fat spreads are suitable for spreading on bread but unsuitable for frying or baking because of their high water content.

Functional dairy spreads contain added plant stanol or sterol esters, which block the absorption of cholesterol in the small intestine so that more is excreted. Examples are Benecol (plant stanol ester) and Flora pro.activ (plant sterol).
Functional dairy spreads are made from vegetable oil, buttermilk, plant stanol or sterol ester, water and salt. They contain no hydrogenated fat and virtually no trans fatty acids.
The cholesterol-lowering effect depends on eating the spread regularly as part of a healthy diet, and it lowers blood (LDL) cholesterol.
notes.tip: Do not mix the two up. Low-fat means less fat and more water, while functional means added plant stanols or sterols, and a functional spread is not automatically low in fat. Stanols reduce absorption of cholesterol in the gut and do not remove cholesterol already in the blood vessels. Be ready to say why low-fat spreads cannot be used for baking.

notes.b: Data questions give the nutrition figures for several spreads and ask you to judge them. The method is to compare the figures, match them to dietary advice and give a verdict.
points: Compare the energy value per 100 g or per serving of each spread.
Compare total fat, saturated fat, monounsaturated fat and polyunsaturated fat, and the salt content (and omega-3 where it is given) for each spread.
Lower energy and lower total fat suit weight control, and lower saturated fat reduces the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).
Higher monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fat, and a lower saturated fat content, suit a diet aimed at protecting the heart. Lower salt suits blood pressure.
Check the water content and whether the spread is suitable for frying or baking.
Compare butter, a spread and a light spread, and state the fat content differences. A lower fat content follows from a higher water content.
Reach a verdict for each product, such as suiting weight reduction or CHD risk reduction, and give a reason for each judgement that refers to the figures.
notes.tip: Compare energy, total and saturated fat, polyunsaturated fat and salt of the products against current dietary advice, and reach a verdict for each one.

keyTerms.definition: A scraped-surface heat exchanger that chills and churns margarine into a plastic fat.
The water-based part of an emulsion, such as the water and milk in margarine.
Adding vitamins or minerals to a food that does not contain them naturally, such as vitamins A and D to margarine.
A spread with less fat and more water than butter or margarine, which is unsuitable for frying or baking.
A spread with added plant stanol or sterol esters that reduce the absorption of cholesterol.
A plant-derived compound added to spreads that blocks cholesterol absorption in the small intestine.
The last date on which a perishable food, such as a fresh spread, should be eaten.
The panel on a food label that states the energy and nutrient content per 100 g or per portion.

questions.prompt: State two nutrients added to margarine through fortification, and explain the role of each in the body.
questions.model: Vitamin A: supports vision, growth and the immune system. Vitamin D: helps the body absorb calcium and maintain healthy bones. Award one mark for each nutrient named and up to two marks for each explanation, to a maximum of 6.

questions.prompt: Outline the stages in the production of margarine, and describe the information a consumer can find on its label.
questions.model: Vegetable oil is extracted and refined, then hydrogen is added at the double bonds using a nickel catalyst to produce a semi-solid fat. The oils are blended and the water phase is prepared with milk or water, salt, colour, flavour, and vitamins A and D. Lecithin is added as an emulsifier, and the emulsion is churned and chilled in a votator to form a plastic fat. The margarine is weighed and packed in foil or plastic tubs. The label gives the name of the product, the ingredients in descending order by weight, allergens, the net quantity, a nutrition declaration per 100 g, a use-by date, storage instructions and the business name and address. Labelling follows Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 as given effect by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
